message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I did the right thing or not in this situation. Let me start by understanding what happened. A few years ago, I was renting a place with this dude. We were on a lease, which means we had a legal agreement to rent the place for a certain period. When the lease was almost up, he just left without giving much notice. He took most of his stuff, but left a few things and a note saying he didn't want to bring those things with him. Now, where I live, if you don't get rid of your stuff when you move out, the landlord can pay someone to remove it, and they can take money from your deposit for that. I've heard of people losing $250 just because someone had to take three milk crates of their stuff to the dump. That's a rip-off. So, I tried to contact him for two weeks, texting and emailing, asking him to pick up his stuff or let me take them to the dump. But he never responded. I ended up taking most of his stuff to the dump, but he had around 60 video games for the PS4. I thought, "Why not sell them?" There's a local game store that buys used games, and they gave me $600 for all of his games. Fast forward to last week, I saw him at a party. We were being polite, but then he asked how the move-out went and what I did with his stuff. When he found out I sold his games, he got mad. I told him I tried to get him to take his stuff, but he never reached out. Now he's calling me an asshole and asking me to pay him back. I checked, and legally, there's nothing I did wrong, but now I'm wondering if I'm the asshole for doing this. Okay, so I need to figure out if I did the right thing or not. Let's break it down. First, legally, I didn't do anything wrong. The landlord can charge for removal if the tenant doesn't take their stuff, and I followed through by trying to contact him. I gave him two weeks to respond, which seems reasonable. When he didn't, I took the stuff to the dump, which is what the landlord would have done anyway, but I saved him from potentially losing money from his deposit. But then, I sold his games and made $600. Is that okay? I mean, legally, I think it's fine because the games were his property, but by not responding, he effectively abandoned them. So, in that sense, I took possession of his abandoned property and sold it. But is that morally right? I think about it this way: if someone abandons their stuff, do I have the right to sell it? Or should I just dispose of it without benefiting from it? I guess legally, I could argue that I was acting in his best interest by not letting the landlord charge him for removal, but morally, taking his stuff and selling it for my own gain feels a bit off. Also, he's upset because he found out about the sale. He feels like I took advantage of him. Even though I tried to contact him, maybe I should have handled it differently. Maybe I should have just thrown the stuff away instead of selling it, even if I lost out on the money. On the other hand, I did try to contact him, and he didn't respond. So, in a way, he gave up his right to his stuff by not responding. But still, selling his stuff without his consent feels like a breach of trust, even if it's legally permissible. I'm also thinking about the practical side. If I hadn't sold the games, I would have had to pay to have them disposed of, which would have cost me money. By selling them, I actually saved myself from that expense and made some money. But does that justify selling his stuff without his permission? I guess it's a tricky situation. Legally, I'm in the clear, but morally, it's a bit gray. I did what I thought was necessary to prevent financial loss for both of us, but I also took advantage of his inaction to benefit myself. That might be why he's upset. Maybe I should have handled it differently. Perhaps I could have stored his stuff somewhere until he responded, but that would have been inconvenient and costly. Or maybe I could have donated the games instead of selling them, but then I wouldn't have made the money. In the end, I think I did what I thought was best under the circumstances, but I can see why he feels wronged. It's a tough spot to be in, and I can understand his frustration.
